mastery.oneLine: A step-by-step orthopedic examination that decides first whether a joint needs mobilizing, stabilizing or something else, then treats and retests.
mastery.whatItIs: The Paris approach, associated with Stanley Paris, is a framework for orthopedic manual therapy. You examine in a set order, classify the problem (for example hypomobile, hypermobile or not mechanical), choose joint-specific treatment, and teach exercises for lasting change.
mastery.analogy: Like a mechanic who diagnoses with a checklist before touching any bolt. The checking is the skill; the spanner comes later.
coreIdeas: Examine before you treat: history, observation, active and passive movement, joint-play and neurological checks, in a consistent order.
Treat according to the finding: stiff joints may be mobilized, loose joints need stabilizing exercise.
Retest the functional problem and build active rehabilitation around it.

terms.meaning: A joint moving less than expected.
A joint moving more than expected; usually needs stability, not stretching.
Small passive movements of a joint surface the patient cannot do actively.
Grouping the problem to guide treatment choice.
Using findings to decide and revise the plan.

whenToUse: Joint or spine problems where you need a clear reason for choosing manual therapy.
whenNot: When red flags need medical review first.
As a rigid recipe: the order serves the patient, not the other way round.

steps.title: Listen and screen
steps.detail: Take the history and rule out red flags.

steps.title: Observe and test active movement
steps.detail: Watch the movement and note where pain or limitation occurs.

steps.title: Test passive movement and joint play
steps.detail: Check range, end-feel and small glides, comparing sides.

steps.title: Check nerves, muscles and neighbouring joints
steps.detail: The problem may come from elsewhere.

steps.title: Classify and choose
steps.detail: Stiff joint: consider mobilization. Loose joint: stabilize. Unclear: refer or gather more data.

steps.title: Treat, retest and teach
steps.detail: Apply the treatment, retest the movement, and give exercises.

mastery.dose: No fixed dose. Dose follows the technique you choose (for example mobilization grades) and the patient's irritability.

example.patient: Daniel, 55, architect, shoulder stiffness for weeks.
example.assessment: Active and passive elevation are both limited with a firm end-feel; the glide of the joint is reduced; the neck and nerves are clear.
example.treatment: A hypomobile pattern is identified, so joint mobilization and stretching are chosen, plus home exercises.
example.reassess: Elevation improves and he returns to lifting tasks. Had the examination shown a loose joint, stabilizing exercises would have been chosen.

mistakes: Treating the diagram instead of the examination.
mastery.recap: Examine, classify, treat to match, retest.
mastery.evidence: The Paris approach is a reasoning framework, not one treatment. Its components (manual therapy plus exercise) have varying evidence depending on the condition.

depth.why: The Paris tradition is a way of reasoning more than a single technique: a full orthopedic examination (history, active and passive movement, accessory movement, palpation, neurological and special tests) decides whether a joint-specific technique is justified, which one, and how hard. Treatment is a trial: apply it, retest the same comparable sign and keep only what changes it. That discipline is the transferable value; branded protocols do not carry separate proof of superiority.
choose: Use the framework whenever a joint restriction, not pain alone, is the reason for considering mobilization.
Prefer an active or education-led plan when the examination shows no joint-specific restriction or when symptoms are highly irritable.
Choose the technique (graded oscillation, sustained stretch or a thrust) from irritability and end-feel, not from the name of the school.
Combine every joint technique with active movement and loading so the new range is used.
parameters: History, active and passive range, accessory movement, palpation, a neurological screen and a comparable sign before any technique
A short bout of a graded technique, then retest the comparable sign; repeat only if it improved
Chosen by irritability: gentle oscillations when irritable, sustained or end-range stretch when stiff and not irritable
Active range, motor control and loading in the same session
depth.progress: Move from the passive technique to active range, then loaded function. Stop passive treatment as soon as the comparable sign no longer changes with it, and review the diagnosis if two or three trials give no gain, rather than repeating the same technique harder.
measure: The comparable sign (a painful movement or a range) measured the same way before and after each trial
Segmental findings re-palpated, remembering that their reliability between examiners is limited
Function: the patient's own task, retested at the end of the session
depth.evidence: The framework is a reasoning approach, not a tested treatment. Joint mobilization can help selected musculoskeletal problems in the short term, but that evidence belongs to mobilization in general and is not proof for every Paris-branded protocol.
pitfalls: Letting the name of a school choose the technique instead of the examination.
Treating a palpated stiffness as the cause without testing whether treating it changes the patient's sign.
Skipping the retest, so habit is mistaken for a treatment effect.
Stopping at the passive technique and sending the patient away without active work.
screen: Instability, suspected fracture, infection or unexplained serious symptoms

urdu.short: Paris approach ek systematic orthopedic examination framework hai: pehle history aur movement check, phir problem ki classification, us ke mutabiq treatment aur dobara test. Treatment ka intikhab examination ke baad hota hai.

details.heading: Yeh kya hai?
details.text: Stanley Paris se associated yeh framework orthopedic manual therapy mein examination ko ek munazzam order mein rakhta hai. Problem ko classify karke, misal ke taur par hypomobile, hypermobile ya non-mechanical, joint-specific treatment aur long-term change ke liye exercises choose ki jati hain.

details.heading: Misal se samjhein
details.text: Yeh mechanic ki tarah hai jo bolt chhoone se pehle checklist se problem diagnose karta hai. Asal skill checking mein hai; spanner baad mein aata hai.

details.heading: Bunyadi ideas
details.text: Treatment se pehle history, observation, active/passive movement, joint play aur neurological checks karein. Stiff joint ko mobilization ki zaroorat ho sakti hai, jabke loose joint ko stabilizing exercise chahiye ho sakti hai. Functional problem ko retest karke active rehabilitation banayein.

details.heading: Aham terms
details.text: Hypomobile: joint expected se kam move karta hai. Hypermobile: expected se zyada move karta hai; aam tor par stretching ke bajaye stability chahiye hoti hai. Joint play: joint surfaces ki chhoti passive movement jo patient khud active taur par nahi karta. Classification: findings ke mutabiq problem ko group karna. Clinical reasoning: findings se plan banana aur zaroorat par badalna.

details.heading: Kab use karein / kab nahi
details.text: Joint ya spine problems mein jab manual therapy choose karne ki clear wajah chahiye, aur systematic examination sikhane ke liye. Red flags hon to pehle medical review karein. Isay rigid recipe na banayein; sequence patient ki zaroorat ke liye hai.

details.heading: Steps
details.text:
1. History lein aur red flags screen karein.
2. Active movement observe karke pain aur limitation note karein.
3. Passive movement aur joint play, range, end-feel aur small glides assess karein.
4. Nerves, muscles aur nearby joints check karein.
5. Findings classify karein: stiffness mein mobilization consider ho sakti hai; laxity mein stabilization; unclear case mein aur data ya referral.
6. Treatment ke baad retest karein aur exercise sikhayein.

details.heading: Dose
details.text: Koi fixed dose nahi. Dose chosen technique, jaise mobilization grade, aur patient ki irritability ke mutabiq hoti hai.

details.heading: Clinical example — source ka scenario
details.text: Source mein Daniel, 55 saal ke architect, ke shoulder mein hafton se stiffness hai. Active aur passive elevation dono limited, firm end-feel aur reduced joint glide milta hai; neck aur nerves ke checks clear hain. Hypomobile pattern ke mutabiq mobilization, stretching aur home exercises choose ki jati hain. Retest par elevation behtar hoti hai. Agar joint loose hota to stabilization exercise choose hoti. Yeh teaching scenario hai, universal treatment recommendation nahi.

details.heading: Aam ghaltiyan
details.text: Examination ke bajaye diagram ko follow karna; hypermobile joint mobilize karna; aur retest skip karna.

details.heading: Self-test
details.text: Hypermobile joint ko mobilize ya stabilize? Stabilize. Treatment choose karne se pehle kya zaroori hai? Systematic examination.

details.heading: Recap aur evidence
details.text: Examine karein, classify karein, finding ke mutabiq treatment dein aur retest karein. Paris approach reasoning framework hai, ek single treatment nahi. Is ke components ki evidence condition ke mutabiq mukhtalif hoti hai.

deeper.heading: Approach ka overview
deeper.text: Paris approach manual therapy ko examination, joint mechanics, clinical reasoning aur graded intervention ke framework mein dekhta hai. Isay sirf aik specific hand technique samajhne ke bajaye assessment se treatment aur reassessment tak ka process samjhein.

deeper.heading: Clinical decision-making
deeper.text: Patient history, irritability, movement restriction aur functional goals se decide karein ke manual therapy relevant hai ya nahi. Treatment ka choice assessment se justify hona chahiye, na ke therapist ki favourite technique se.

deeper.heading: Common mistakes aur reassessment
deeper.text: Mechanical findings ko patient ke symptoms se alag interpret karna, repeated treatment without retest aur exercise/education ko ignore karna avoid karein. Meaningful movement aur function ko pre/post compare karein.

deeper.heading: Evidence aur patient-centred care
deeper.text: Kisi named approach ka label effectiveness guarantee nahi karta. Individual technique ke evidence, patient preference aur overall rehabilitation plan ko weigh karein; uncertainty ko transparent rakhein.

cue.wake: A pretty joint diagram is not the patient's biography.
cue.question: If the chosen glide doesn't help but an active reach does, what should lead the plan?
cue.answer: The patient's actual task response; change the hypothesis.
cue.easy: Accessory movement = a small joint movement not usually done on its own.

worldDeep.opening: A patient brings a perfect drawing of shoulder joint mechanics. Unfortunately, their shoulder has not read the drawing. The Paris tradition becomes interesting at precisely this moment: when the examiner must decide what the patient’s body actually demonstrates, rather than forcing a prescribed glide onto it. The method is best learned as a sequence of questions: what is happening, what might explain it, which findings are dependable, what is safe, and what changes after a measured intervention?

principles.title: A complete orthopedic examination comes before an elegant technique
principles.body: Start with the story, medical screening, the patient's goal, and the aggravating movement. Ask how symptoms began, what changes them, whether they travel or disturb sleep, and which daily activity should improve. A therapist who starts by choosing a glide before examining the patient has read the final page before the mystery begins.

principles.title: The joint is a system, not a single stiff hinge
principles.body: Distinguish physiological movement the patient can perform from accessory movement that an examiner explores. Consider arthrokinematics, capsular patterns, tissue irritability, muscle control, neural contributions and adjacent regions. Small glide and spin relationships may inform a hypothesis, but are not directly observable with certainty from touch alone.

principles.title: Compare active, passive, resisted and functional findings
principles.body: An active motion may be limited by pain, weakness, confidence or mechanical stiffness. Passive testing can explore available motion and symptom quality, while suitable resisted tests help assess contractile contributions. No single test identifies every lesion. Patterns and consistency matter more than one dramatic positive finding.

principles.title: Clinical reasoning outranks school loyalty
principles.body: A Paris-style rationale can guide a selective manual input, but the label on a treatment school does not establish treatment superiority. The examiner uses the hypothesis, explains the uncertainty, gains consent and evaluates whether an appropriately low-risk trial changes a comparable sign.

principles.title: Reassessment closes the reasoning loop
principles.body: Repeat the same reach, turn, squat or transfer under comparable conditions. Note direction, pain, range, quality and carryover. If movement is easier, active practice can consolidate that window. If not, change the hypothesis rather than declaring that the patient needs a stronger version of the favorite technique.

assessment.title: History and screening
assessment.body: Clarify onset, trauma, systemic features, neurologic symptoms, vascular risk where relevant, irritability, medications, prior interventions and patient priorities. Suspected fracture, infection, serious neurologic loss or instability makes routine mobilization inappropriate.

assessment.title: Movement examination
assessment.body: Observe familiar functional tasks first; then compare active and appropriately selected passive motion. Document the baseline clearly enough that a colleague could repeat it. Record movement quality and pain behavior instead of only saying 'stiff'.

assessment.title: Joint-play interpretation
assessment.body: When suitable and within training, explore accessory motion with consistent support and light, graded input. Perceived stiffness is a subjective examination finding, not a diagnosis of microscopic subluxation. Combine it with other clinical findings.

assessment.title: Choosing the intervention
assessment.body: Match technique to the presentation's irritability and goals, with explicit informed consent. Set a stop rule before starting and pair any useful change with patient participation—movement, strengthening or activity modification.

application.title: 1. Make the problem observable
application.body: Ask the patient to demonstrate one specific difficult action. For shoulder restriction, an overhead shelf reach can be more useful than the phrase 'joint tightness'. Note what stops the movement and whether symptoms travel.

application.title: 2. Form two competing explanations
application.body: For example, consider a mobility-related limitation versus weakness or pain-related guarding. Check what would distinguish them through safe active, passive and appropriate resisted testing. This prevents premature diagnosis by palpation.

application.title: 3. Choose a precise, safe trial
application.body: A trained clinician supports the relevant joint, controls the adjacent segment and selects a tolerable accessory direction or another appropriate intervention. The exact contact, grade, direction and dose depend on the joint, irritability and specialist training; no universal glide fits every patient.

application.title: 4. Explain the why without promising magic
application.body: Tell the patient you are testing whether a controlled mechanical and sensory input makes their chosen movement more comfortable. Do not claim to reposition a bone or break invisible adhesions.

application.title: 5. Remove the hands and retest
application.body: Ask for exactly the same movement and measure changes in range, symptom behavior and confidence. If the effect is useful, rehearse the newly comfortable task actively. If not, make an explicit new clinical choice.

application.title: 6. Document and plan
application.body: Record baseline, intervention purpose, response, adverse reactions and the next functional goal. Review whether the change survives outside the clinic rather than ending the story with a beautiful treatment-table performance.

caseStudy.scene: An architect arrives with shoulder discomfort and an illustrated joint-glide chart. He tries to reach the highest shelf, then offers to supervise the therapist's hand direction. The shoulder appears to have appointed itself a project manager.
caseStudy.findings: The overhead reach is painful near the top, yet there is also weakness and increased guarding. Passive motion is less restricted than the patient's active reach. Those findings challenge the assumption that a single capsular glide is the whole answer.
caseStudy.decision: The therapist screens the shoulder, explores comfortable movement and chooses a low-risk trial matched to irritability. A strengthening and graded-reaching component is planned from the start. The chart is thanked for its service but not promoted to consultant.
caseStudy.twist: The selected manual input produces little immediate change. A supported, load-adjusted active reach performs better. The initial favorite joint-play hypothesis is revised instead of defended.
caseStudy.finish: The patient leaves with a safe progression for reaching and a way to measure change at home. The lesson is not 'Paris always uses this glide'; it is 'assessment determines the trial and reassessment determines the next step'.

worldDeep.dose: There is no single 'Paris dosage.' Joint direction, oscillatory or sustained input, force and repetitions must be specified for the actual joint and clinical purpose by a qualified clinician. Highly irritable presentations usually warrant a more cautious strategy; record the response and stop for worsening symptoms.
worldDeep.caution: Do not use forceful joint mobilization with suspected instability, fracture, active infection, severe osteoporosis-related fragility or serious unexplained neurologic findings. For cervical complaints, current vascular/neurologic screening and informed consent are essential. The patient's improvement never licenses unsafe force.

evidence.known: Condition-specific clinical guidelines sometimes support selected joint mobilization as part of multimodal rehabilitation. Functional outcome assessment, progressive exercise and patient-centered education are widely transferable priorities.
evidence.unknown: No clinical trial of general joint mobilization validates every historic Paris interpretation, every hand placement or a specific grade for every individual. Joint-play palpation cannot reliably prove a precisely 'misaligned' bone.
evidence.communication: 'We are going to test one carefully chosen input against the movement you want back. If it helps, we will use that opportunity to practice. If it doesn't, we reconsider—your shoulder does not have to agree with my diagram.'

worldDeep.memoryHook: The diagram is a map. The examination is the compass. The patient's task is the destination.

checks.question: An accessory glide feels stiff but passive and active function are normal. What is the danger of treating the palpation as the diagnosis?
checks.answer: A subjective joint-play finding alone may have poor diagnostic specificity. Use symptoms, function, other examination findings and clinical goals before deciding whether intervention is justified.

checks.question: Why does immediate retesting matter after a manual trial?
checks.answer: It checks the original comparable sign under similar conditions and helps avoid confusing therapist sensation with a change that matters to the patient.
